extracted.intended_audience: public relations professionals and media relations practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for PR practitioners on how to craft, time, and format pitches to journalists based on a survey of 2,000+ journalists. Focuses on channel, timing, length, subject lines, common mistakes, and source readiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preferred pitching channels
rubrics_metrics.description: Email: 96% prefer; LinkedIn message: 30%; Twitter/X DM: 22%; Phone call: 5% (mostly broadcast); Snail mail: 1%.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Email is overwhelmingly preferred — prioritize email outreach. Use LinkedIn or X DMs less often; phone calls are mainly appropriate for broadcast reporters; avoid snail mail except in rare circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best time to pitch
rubrics_metrics.description: Morning (5-8am ET): 50% open rate; Mid-morning (9-11am): 35%; Afternoon: 20%; Evening / weekend: <10%.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Send pitches in the early morning window (roughly 5–8am ET) to maximize open rates; avoid evenings and weekends when open rates fall below 10%.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optimal pitch length
rubrics_metrics.description: Under 200 words: 73% read; 200-400 words: 52% read; 400+ words: 23% read.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep pitches concise — aim for under 200 words to achieve the highest read rate. Longer pitches see sharply diminished readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject line preferences
rubrics_metrics.description: "Story idea about [specific topic]" — 45% open; "Exclusive: [news]" — 40% open (only if true); "[News] — quick interview opportunity" — 38%; "Press release: [headline]" — 18%; "Hi [Name]" — 8%.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use specific, news-focused subject lines that present a clear story idea or a timely interview opportunity. Avoid generic greetings or simply labeling something as a press release; only use 'Exclusive' when it is genuinely exclusive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Things journalists want PR pros to stop doing
rubrics_metrics.description: Following up more than once (62%); Mass-blasting the same pitch (58%); Pitching irrelevant beats (55%); Sending PDF-only attachments (43%); Using "exclusive" inaccurately (40%); Vague subject lines (38%).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid repetitive follow-ups, mass email blasts, pitching reporters outside their beats, sending assets only as PDFs, misusing 'exclusive', and writing vague subject lines — these are top annoyances and reduce pickup chances.

rubrics_metrics.name: What journalists want more of
rubrics_metrics.description: Data and original research (78%); Diverse expert sources (65%); Embargoed exclusives (52%); Visual assets ready to use (49%); Quick-turnaround sources (42%).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pitch with original data or research when possible, include diverse expert sources, offer embargoed exclusives when appropriate, attach ready-to-use visuals, and provide sources who can respond quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: What makes a source re-quotable
rubrics_metrics.description: Available within 24 hours; Quotable in clear, jargon-free language; Provides specific examples; Honest about limitations of expertise; No PR rep gatekeeping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make sure sources can respond rapidly, speak plainly with concrete examples, acknowledge limitations, and allow journalists to quote them directly without heavy PR mediation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Muck Rack quality rubric for pitches
rubrics_metrics.description: Email format; Sent during morning hours; Under 200 words; Specific subject line with story idea; Personalized to beat; Visual assets attached; Source genuinely available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distilled checklist summarizes the survey's top criteria — aim to meet each item (email + morning timing + concise + specific subject + personalized targeting + visual assets + available source) to maximize the chance a pitch is read and used.
